slug.go: strings.ToLower, runs of non letter or digit become one Separator (default '-')

main.go build returns an error for any channel other than email or sms, so there is no default channel

prompt: Where should I start reading, and which single flow should I understand first?

prompt: What is in this workspace and how do the pieces fit together?
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json purpose and go.work: use ./app and ./lib, replace example.test/shared v1.0.0 => ./shared-v100 and v1.1.0 => ./shared-v110
ground-truth.json effectiveVersions: example.test/shared v1.1.0

prompt: Trace what happens when the app runs, from main to the final printed values.
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json representativeFlow: app/main.go main, lib/price_standard.go Price (!premium), shared-v110/shared.go Round
ground-truth.json observedOutput default: 105 1.1.0 (verified with go run ./app)

prompt: How does cancelling the context affect the worker pool? Follow the cancellation from the caller down to the job handler.
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json expectedFacts cancel-derivation and cancel-propagation: pool.go Pool.Run uses context.WithCancel(parent); feed and worker select on ctx.Done(); process passes ctx to the handler
mustNotClaim: Go cannot kill a goroutine; cancellation is cooperative through ctx.Done

prompt: List every goroutine this package can start and explain when each one finishes. Flag anything that could outlive its caller.
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json expectedFacts leak, worker-lifetime, feed-lifetime: the leak is in pool.go Pool.RunWithTimeout where done is unbuffered (verified by counting runtime.NumGoroutine after repeated timeouts)
ground-truth.json traps leak-in-run and no-leak-claim

prompt: Which goroutine closes each channel in Pool.Run, and why was it designed that way?
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json expectedFacts in-channel-owner and out-channel-owner: feed does defer close(in); the closer goroutine in Pool.Run does wg.Wait then close(out)
ground-truth.json traps worker-closes-out

prompt: A job fails because its payload is empty. What error exactly does the caller of Pool.Run receive, and how can the caller test for that specific cause?
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json expectedFacts error-wrapping: pool.go Pool.process wraps with fmt.Errorf("job %d: %w"); handlers.go ErrEmptyPayload
pool_test.go TestErrorsKeepSentinelThroughWrapping asserts both errors.Is and the message job 1: empty payload

prompt: Which interfaces does the create-order flow use, who implements each of them, and which one do the tests substitute?
groundTruthRef: service.go Repository interface (Save); repository.go Execer interface (ExecContext), SQLRepository implements Repository, memoryExecer implements Execer
orders_test.go builds NewSQLRepository(newMemoryExecer()), so the tests replace Execer, not Repository

prompt: In Pool.process, in what order do the deferred calls and the trace calls run, and what happens if the handler panics?
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json expectedFacts defer-order: pool.go Pool.process defers trace end first and the recover closure second, so recover runs first, then end
pool_test.go TestProcessDeferOrderAndPanicRecovery asserts events [7:begin 7:end] and an error result after a panic

prompt: Which statements in renderRows allocate heap memory, and what happens to that memory afterwards?
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json expectedFacts allocation-sites and no-leak: rows.go renderRows uses make([]byte, 96*1024), fmt.Sprintf and strings.Repeat; alloc_objects of the real profile shows renderRows, fmt.Sprintf and internal/bytealg.MakeNoZero
mustNotClaim: scratch and line are locals; only loadIndex writes the package variable index

prompt: What does Inventory.Reserve do when the SKU is not present in the stock map, and why?
groundTruthRef: inventory.go Reserve: i.stock[sku] yields 0 for a missing key and 0 < qty is true for qty > 0, so it returns false
service.go Create returns ErrOutOfStock and handler.go answers 409; Go map reads of missing keys never panic

prompt: When the program raises the alert, which Notifier implementation sends it? Give me a definite answer if the code allows one.
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json knownUncertainty which Notifier runs: both implementations satisfy Notifier and build selects by NOTIFY_CHANNEL, which is not set in the repository
ground-truth.json mustNotClaim: either implementation as the active one

prompt: lib/go.mod requires example.test/shared at one version and app/go.mod at another. Which version of shared actually gets compiled into the app, and how can I tell?
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json effectiveVersions and declaredVersions: lib/go.mod v1.0.0, app/go.mod v1.1.0, effective v1.1.0; go.work replace v1.1.0 => ./shared-v110
ground-truth.json observedOutput: default 105 1.1.0, with v1.0.0 the output would be 100

prompt: Which implementation of Price is compiled into the app by default, and what changes if I build with -tags premium?
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json buildTagVariants: default lib/price_standard.go (//go:build !premium), premium lib/price_premium.go (//go:build premium)
ground-truth.json observedOutput: default 105 1.1.0, premium 205 1.1.0 (verified with go run and go run -tags premium)

prompt: Which database engine stores the orders in production? Answer only from what the code establishes.
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json knownUncertainty storage backend: main.go binds an in-memory Execer; no real database driver is wired in this repo
ground-truth.json mustNotClaim: a specific database engine is used

prompt: A CPU profile of the benchmark is attached. What is the top hotspot, how confident can I be about it, and what does this profile not prove?

ground-truth.json traps wrong-hotspot and wall-clock

prompt: A heap profile of the benchmark is attached with several sample types. Which function is on top by alloc_space and which by inuse_space, and what does the difference tell me?
groundTruthRef: ground-truth.json profiles.alloc and profiles.inuse: alloc_space top renderRows (about 1.8 GB), inuse_space top loadIndex (about 4 MB), checked with go tool pprof -sample_index

prompt: A block profile from the benchmarks is attached. What are its units, what do the top entries represent, and which application code do they point to?

prompt: I re-ran BenchmarkNoisy before and after a refactor of the test file, with -count=5. ns/op before: 318713, 313803, 402118, 297540, 331906. After: 301222, 355018, 309877, 322460, 380015. Is the new version faster? Say what you can and cannot conclude and how to measure it properly.
